Privileges of Rajya Sabha and Its Members (Articles 105 and 194)

solution.concept_anchor: Disqualifications — Tenth Schedule applies equally to Rajya Sabha

statement_analysis.statement: The Tenth Schedule (anti-defection law) applies to members of the Lok Sabha but not to members of the Rajya Sabha, as the latter are elected by state legislatures and are expected to exercise independent judgment.
statement_analysis.reason: The Tenth Schedule applies equally to members of both Houses of Parliament — Rajya Sabha members are fully subject to disqualification for defection, and the Chairman of Rajya Sabha (not the Speaker) is the relevant authority for deciding such questions.

statement_analysis.statement: A Rajya Sabha member who is found to be of unsound mind by a competent court is disqualified under Article 102 — the same disqualification that applies to Lok Sabha members.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 102 prescribes identical disqualifications for both Houses — holding office of profit, unsound mind (declared by competent court), insolvency, non-citizenship, and other disqualifications prescribed by Parliament. Both Houses are treated equally under this provision.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the Tenth Schedule, when a disqualification question arises in relation to a member of the Rajya Sabha, the matter is decided by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
statement_analysis.reason: Disqualification questions under the Tenth Schedule relating to Rajya Sabha members are decided by the Chairman of Rajya Sabha — not the Speaker of Lok Sabha. Each House has its own presiding officer for this purpose.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who correctly identify Statement 1 as incorrect may assume Statement 2 must also be incorrect (following the question's 'NOT correct' framing) and overlook that Statement 2 is actually the one correct statement in the set.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 — Tenth Schedule applies to Rajya Sabha equally; the claim that it does not apply is factually wrong. Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Statement 2 — Article 102 disqualifications apply identically to both Houses; this statement is correct (not a 'NOT correct' candidate).
Statement 3 — Disqualification under Tenth Schedule for Rajya Sabha members is decided by the Chairman, not the Speaker. Statement 3 is NOT correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits a scope-extension myth — that Rajya Sabha members have greater independence because of their indirect election route, and that the anti-defection law should not apply to them. This is constitutionally false. Statement 3 exploits the Speaker's prominence: students know the Speaker decides anti-defection cases and may incorrectly extend this to Rajya Sabha members, forgetting that the Chairman is the equivalent authority there.
solution.final_explanation:
The Tenth Schedule (inserted by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment, 1985) applies to all elected members of Parliament — both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha — without distinction. It imposes disqualification for defection (voluntarily giving up party membership or voting against party directions without prior permission).

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Tenth Schedule applies fully to Rajya Sabha members. The Chairman of Rajya Sabha (not the Speaker) is the deciding authority for Rajya Sabha anti-defection cases.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 102 disqualifications (unsound mind, office of profit, insolvency, non-citizenship) apply identically to both Houses.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Chairman of Rajya Sabha decides disqualification questions under the Tenth Schedule for Rajya Sabha members — the Speaker has jurisdiction only over Lok Sabha members.

Value Addition:
• The 91st Constitutional Amendment (2003) capped the size of the Council of Ministers at 15% of House strength and tightened the anti-defection law.
• Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) upheld the Tenth Schedule's constitutional validity.
• Nominated Rajya Sabha members, if they join a political party more than six months after their nomination, are liable to be disqualified.

solution.concept_anchor: Fourth Schedule — seat allocation basis for States in Rajya Sabha
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who recall that 'Schedule' governs Rajya Sabha seat allocation and associate it with a specific number may confuse the Fourth Schedule with the Third Schedule (oaths and affirmations) or Fifth/Sixth Schedules.
elimination_logic: The Fourth Schedule to the Constitution specifically deals with allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha to States and Union Territories.
Eliminate option (a) — the Third Schedule deals with oaths and affirmations; it has no relation to Rajya Sabha seat allocation.
Eliminate option (b) — the First Schedule lists States and UTs; it does not allocate Rajya Sabha seats.
Eliminate option (d) — the Fifth Schedule deals with Scheduled Areas and Tribes; unrelated to Rajya Sabha composition.
Select option (c) — Fourth Schedule.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The plausible-fabrication trap: all four schedules mentioned sound plausible in the context of federal/state-related provisions. The Third Schedule (oaths), First Schedule (listing states), and Fifth Schedule (Scheduled Areas) all have some constitutional relevance to states. A student who does not precisely recall 'Fourth Schedule = Rajya Sabha seats' may be drawn to the First Schedule (which does list the states) or the Third Schedule.
solution.final_explanation:
The Constitution of India contains 12 Schedules, each dealing with specific constitutional matters. Rajya Sabha's seat allocation to States and Union Territories is governed by the Fourth Schedule.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Third Schedule contains the forms of oaths and affirmations for constitutional functionaries — no connection to Rajya Sabha seat allocation.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The First Schedule lists the names of States and Union Territories and their territories — it does not allocate legislative seats.
• Option (c) — Correct: The Fourth Schedule allocates seats in the Rajya Sabha to States and Union Territories — the correct answer.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Fifth Schedule makes provisions for administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes — entirely unrelated.

Value Addition:
• Uttar Pradesh has the largest Rajya Sabha representation (31 seats) due to population-based allocation.
• Sikkim, Nagaland, and Mizoram have one Rajya Sabha seat each — the minimum for a state.
• The Sixth Schedule deals with administration of tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram.

solution.concept_anchor: Open ballot system — Kuldip Nayar case 2006 timeline
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who broadly know 'domicile removal happened early 2000s' and 'Kuldip Nayar case was around 2005-2007' may get the relative order of events 2 and 3 reversed.
elimination_logic: The 52nd Amendment introducing the Tenth Schedule (anti-defection) happened in 1985 — clearly first among these events.
The Representation of the People (Amendment) Act removing domicile requirement was in 2003 — second.
The Supreme Court's judgment in Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India upholding the open ballot system was in 2006 — third and last.
Correct sequence: Tenth Schedule (1985) → Domicile removal (2003) → Kuldip Nayar judgment (2006). This matches option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is the temporal proximity of 2003 and 2006 — events within the same decade. Students who recall both events happened 'in the 2000s' may reverse them, placing Kuldip Nayar before domicile removal. The correct temporal sequence requires knowing the specific years: RP Amendment Act 2003 came before the Supreme Court judgment in 2006.
solution.final_explanation:
Three legislative and judicial developments shaped Rajya Sabha membership and election rules over two decades.

1985: The 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act introduced the Tenth Schedule (anti-defection law) — the earliest event, applicable to both Houses of Parliament including Rajya Sabha.
2003: The Representation of the People (Amendment) Act, 2003 removed the domicile requirement for Rajya Sabha candidates — a person could now represent any state without residing there.
2006: The Supreme Court in Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India upheld the open ballot system in Rajya Sabha elections introduced to check cross-voting — the most recent of the three.

Correct sequence: 1985 → 2003 → 2006 → Option (c).

Value Addition:
• The open ballot system requires Rajya Sabha voters (MLAs) to show their marked ballot to their party agent — uniquely exposing voting choices unlike the secret ballot in general elections.
• The 52nd Amendment (1985) was later modified by the 91st Amendment (2003) which, among other things, tightened anti-defection provisions.
• Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India is also significant for its ruling that open ballot does not violate the secrecy of voting guaranteed under the Constitution.

solution.concept_anchor: Rajya Sabha as federal chamber — paradox of national-interest exclusive powers

statement_analysis.statement: Rajya Sabha's special power under Article 249 to extend Parliament's legislative jurisdiction to State List subjects is aimed at protecting State interests by ensuring the States' representative body consents before Parliament encroaches on State legislative domain.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 249 is framed in terms of 'national interest' — not state protection. The resolution under Article 249 actually enables Parliament to encroach on state legislative subjects; it does not protect states. This is the constitutional paradox: an institution called 'Council of States' exercises a power that overrides state autonomy in the name of national interest.

statement_analysis.statement: Unlike the United States Senate, the Rajya Sabha does not operate on the principle of equal representation for all States — its seat allocation is population-based, making it less effective as a protector of smaller States' interests.
statement_analysis.reason: The Fourth Schedule allocates seats based on population; smaller states have fewer seats. This directly weakens Rajya Sabha's federal character compared to the US Senate's equal two-seats-per-state model.

statement_analysis.statement: Both Article 249 and Article 312 are powers that Rajya Sabha exercises as a representative of States, but paradoxically both powers operate in the national interest and can override or affect state administrative autonomy.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 249 allows Parliament to legislate on State List subjects (directly overriding state legislative exclusivity) and Article 312 allows creation of All-India Services that serve in state cadres — both are exercises of national interest powers, not state protection powers, creating the constitutional paradox.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who accept Statement 1 as a reasonable summary of Article 249's purpose (states' consent = state protection) may mark it correct and select option (b) or (d) without noticing the 'national interest' versus 'state protection' distinction.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 — Article 249 is a national interest power; it enables Parliamentary encroachment on state subjects, not protection of state interests. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Statement 2 — Population-based allocation confirmed by Fourth Schedule; contrast with US Senate's equal representation. Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 3 — Both Articles 249 and 312 are national-interest powers that paradoxically override state autonomy. Statement 3 is correct.
Only Statements 2 and 3 are correct — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 is the most subtle trap in this question. It uses the language of 'state consent' and 'States' representative body' to make an Article 249 resolution sound like it protects states. In reality, Article 249 is a mechanism for Parliament to override state legislative exclusivity — the opposite of state protection. A student who conflates 'Rajya Sabha as states' representative' with 'Rajya Sabha always protects states' will mark Statement 1 correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Rajya Sabha is formally titled the 'Council of States' but its relationship with actual state protection is constitutionally complex.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Article 249 is a national interest override power, not a state protection mechanism. Rajya Sabha's resolution under Article 249 enables Parliament to invade state legislative domains — the opposite of protecting states.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Population-based seat allocation under the Fourth Schedule means large states dominate Rajya Sabha; smaller states have fewer seats. This is unlike the US Senate (2 seats per state regardless of size).
• Statement 3 — Correct: Articles 249 and 312 both describe Rajya Sabha acting in the national interest — enabling parliamentary encroachment (Article 249) and creating services serving state cadres (Article 312). Both paradoxically affect state autonomy despite emanating from the 'states' house.'

Value Addition:
• This paradox is described by scholars as Rajya Sabha being a 'national chamber with a federal label' rather than a genuinely federal upper house.
• A truly federal Rajya Sabha would require equal state representation and a strong state-protective veto — India rejected both.
• The German Bundesrat is composed of state government representatives who vote on block by state — a model closer to genuine federalism than India's Rajya Sabha.

solution.concept_anchor: Chairman casting vote — Article 100 application to Rajya Sabha
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students may confuse the casting vote with an ordinary vote; the Chairman has a casting vote but not a vote in the first instance — selecting option (a) reflects this confusion.
elimination_logic: Article 100(1): Every question in Parliament is decided by a majority of votes of members present and voting, other than the Speaker/Chairman.
The Speaker/Chairman does not vote in the first instance — they vote only to resolve a tie (casting vote).
Eliminate option (a) — the Chairman can vote in case of tie (casting vote), but not in the first instance.
Eliminate option (c) — the Vice-President does not lose voting rights as Vice-President; the restriction is as Chairman of Rajya Sabha during presiding.
Select option (b) — the Chairman does not vote in the first instance but has a casting vote to resolve a tie.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap conflates the Chairman's role with an ordinary member's voting rights. Students who know 'the Speaker cannot vote' may not apply this precisely to the Chairman of Rajya Sabha and may confuse the casting vote with a complete absence of voting rights. Option (a) — that the Chairman votes in all proceedings — reverses the constitutional position.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 100(1) governs voting in both Houses of Parliament. The presiding officer — Speaker in Lok Sabha, Chairman in Rajya Sabha — does not vote in the first instance. If votes are tied equally, the presiding officer exercises a casting vote to break the deadlock.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Chairman (Vice-President) votes in all proceedings as a full member. This is wrong — the Chairman cannot vote in the first instance.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Chairman does not vote initially but casts a deciding vote in the event of a tie. This applies equally when the Deputy Chairman presides in the Chairman's absence.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The restriction is as Chairman of Rajya Sabha; it relates to the presiding role, not the Vice-Presidency. The Vice-President has no separate parliamentary voting right.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The casting vote rule applies only in case of a tie; it is not a vote on every bill as a matter of course.

Value Addition:
• The casting vote is a constitutional power, not merely a convention — it is expressly conferred by Article 100(1).
• A casting vote by the presiding officer typically favours the status quo — rejecting the motion — by convention.
• The same casting vote rule applies to the Deputy Chairman when presiding over Rajya Sabha proceedings.

solution.concept_anchor: Emergency approvals — Rajya Sabha permanence and solo approval role

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 356, if Lok Sabha is dissolved after a proclamation of President's Rule is issued but before the proclamation is approved by Lok Sabha, the Rajya Sabha alone can approve the proclamation, keeping it in force.
statement_analysis.reason: Rajya Sabha's permanent character is constitutionally significant here: Article 356 provides that Rajya Sabha alone can approve President's Rule when Lok Sabha is not available — this is the only emergency type with this specific provision.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 352, if Lok Sabha is dissolved while a national emergency proclamation is in force, the Rajya Sabha may extend the emergency unilaterally without waiting for the reconstituted Lok Sabha to meet.
statement_analysis.reason: Revoking or continuing a national emergency requires both Houses. If Lok Sabha is dissolved while an emergency is in force, the emergency continues but any further approval or continuation resolution must await the reconstituted Lok Sabha — Rajya Sabha cannot unilaterally extend or revoke the emergency.

statement_analysis.statement: The permanent character of Rajya Sabha ensures that committee reports, pending bills introduced in Rajya Sabha, and resolutions adopted by it do not lapse when Lok Sabha is dissolved.
statement_analysis.reason: Because Rajya Sabha is never dissolved, its institutional memory and pending work survive Lok Sabha dissolution — bills at various stages in Rajya Sabha, committee work, and adopted resolutions remain valid until acted upon or superseded.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who reason 'Rajya Sabha's permanence means it can handle all emergencies alone' may mark all three statements correct, extending the solo-approval principle of Article 356 wrongly to Article 352.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 — Article 356 explicitly provides for Rajya Sabha-only approval when Lok Sabha is dissolved; this is constitutionally accurate. Statement 1 is correct.
Statement 2 — National emergency continuation/extension requires both Houses; Rajya Sabha cannot act alone on Article 352 matters when Lok Sabha is dissolved. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 3 — Rajya Sabha permanence means pending business survives Lok Sabha dissolution. Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the trap — students who correctly learn that 'Rajya Sabha alone can approve President's Rule when Lok Sabha is dissolved' may incorrectly generalise this to mean Rajya Sabha can handle all emergencies alone. The provision for solo Rajya Sabha approval is specific to Article 356 only; Article 352 (national emergency) has no equivalent provision.
solution.final_explanation:
Rajya Sabha's permanence creates asymmetric constitutional significance across different emergency types.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 356's approval mechanism allows Rajya Sabha to act alone when Lok Sabha is dissolved — a unique provision reflecting Rajya Sabha's permanent character.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 352 (national emergency) has no equivalent solo-Rajya Sabha provision. Continuation or revocation requires both Houses; if Lok Sabha is dissolved during an emergency, the emergency continues automatically (under existing approval) but new approval resolutions await the reconstituted Lok Sabha.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Rajya Sabha's non-dissolvable nature means its pending work survives Lok Sabha's dissolution — a practical constitutional advantage.

Value Addition:
• President's Rule approved by Rajya Sabha alone (when Lok Sabha is dissolved) remains valid for 30 days from the date of the first sitting of the reconstituted Lok Sabha.
• National Emergency under Article 352 can be revoked only by Lok Sabha passing a resolution — Rajya Sabha plays no role in revocation.
• India has proclaimed National Emergency three times (1962, 1971, 1975) and President's Rule has been imposed over 130 times in various states.

solution.concept_anchor: Committee on Subordinate Legislation — separate committees in each House
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students may assume Parliament has a single unified Committee on Subordinate Legislation that serves both Houses jointly, similar to some select joint committees.
elimination_logic: Rajya Sabha has its own Committee on Subordinate Legislation — separate from Lok Sabha's committee; both Houses have independent committees for scrutinising delegated legislation.
Eliminate option (a) — Rajya Sabha's Committee on Subordinate Legislation is not constitutionally mandated by Article 118; it is a committee under Rules of Procedure, not an Article 118 body.
Eliminate option (b) — There is no unified joint Committee on Subordinate Legislation serving both Houses; each House has its own.
Eliminate option (c) — The Committee on Subordinate Legislation does not have the power to strike down delegated legislation; it can only report to the House, which may then take action.
Select option (d) — Rajya Sabha has its own independent Committee on Subordinate Legislation, separate from Lok Sabha's equivalent committee.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) is a plausible fabrication: students familiar with joint parliamentary committees (like the Joint Committee on Offices of Profit or Joint Committees on specific bills) may assume there is also a Joint Committee on Subordinate Legislation. In reality, each House maintains its own separate Committee on Subordinate Legislation.
solution.final_explanation:
Parliamentary oversight of delegated legislation operates through separate committees in each House — the Committee on Subordinate Legislation of Lok Sabha and the Committee on Subordinate Legislation of Rajya Sabha. They function independently, examining whether rules and regulations framed under statutes are within the delegated authority.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Committee on Subordinate Legislation is not constituted under Article 118 (which deals with rules of procedure generally); it operates under the Rules of Procedure of each House.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: There is no joint Committee on Subordinate Legislation serving both Houses together; the two committees are separate and independent.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Committee on Subordinate Legislation cannot strike down delegated legislation; it examines and reports to the House, which may then pass a resolution or take other action.
• Option (d) — Correct: Rajya Sabha has its own independent Committee on Subordinate Legislation — correctly matched with having a separate, independent function from Lok Sabha's equivalent committee.

Value Addition:
• When a statute says delegated legislation shall be 'subject to modification by Parliament,' both Houses must act — Rajya Sabha cannot be bypassed.
• 'Laying' requirements differ: negative laying (annulment if either House resolves within specified period) vs. affirmative laying (requires active approval).
• The Chairman of Rajya Sabha's Committee on Subordinate Legislation is typically an experienced member with legal background.

solution.concept_anchor: Nominated members — eligibility for ministerial appointment and party membership

statement_analysis.statement: Nominated members of the Rajya Sabha are eligible to be appointed as Ministers in the Union Council of Ministers.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 75(5) read with Article 88 requires Ministers to be members of either House within six months of appointment; nominated members are full members of Rajya Sabha and are constitutionally eligible for ministerial appointments — several nominated members have been appointed Ministers in the past.

statement_analysis.statement: A nominated member of the Rajya Sabha who joins a political party immediately after taking their oath of office is liable to be disqualified under the Tenth Schedule.
statement_analysis.reason: The Tenth Schedule makes a specific exemption for nominated members: a nominated member who was not a member of any political party at the time of nomination may join a political party within six months of taking their seat without incurring disqualification. Joining immediately after oath is therefore NOT a disqualification ground within the six-month window.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know nominated members are full parliamentary members may mark both statements correct without recalling the Tenth Schedule's six-month grace period for nominated members joining a party.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1 — Article 75(5) allows anyone who is a member of Parliament to be a Minister; nominated members are full Rajya Sabha members. Statement 1 is correct.

Check Statement 2 — Tenth Schedule para 2 provides that nominated members may join a party within six months of their first sitting without disqualification. Joining immediately is within the grace period. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (c).

Re-check options: (a) Both correct, (b) Both incorrect, (c) 1 correct 2 incorrect, (d) 1 incorrect 2 correct. Answer is (c). Wait — mapping to the question's options as presented: option (c) here corresponds to 'Statement 1 is correct but Statement 2 is incorrect.' But looking at the correct_option field which says 'b' — let me recheck. The options in this format are: (a) Both correct, (b) Both incorrect, (c) 1 correct 2 incorrect, (d) 1 incorrect 2 correct. The correct answer is (c) since Statement 1 is correct and Statement 2 is incorrect.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the scope-extension trap: students who know nominated members are subject to the Tenth Schedule may extend this to mean 'any party joining causes disqualification.' The specific exception in the Tenth Schedule for nominated members — a six-month grace period to join a party — is the precise knowledge that prevents the wrong answer.
solution.final_explanation:
Nominated members of Rajya Sabha are full members of Parliament with all attendant rights and obligations, subject to one important Tenth Schedule carve-out.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Nominated members are eligible to be appointed Ministers. Article 75(5) requires Ministers to be parliamentarians within six months; nominated Rajya Sabha members satisfy this requirement and have historically been appointed to the Council of Ministers.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Tenth Schedule (Para 2, proviso) grants nominated members a six-month window from their first sitting to join a political party without facing disqualification. Joining immediately after oath is within this window and does not trigger disqualification.

Value Addition:
• After the six-month window expires, a nominated member who joins a party becomes liable to disqualification under the Tenth Schedule.
• Nominated members CAN vote in Vice-Presidential elections but NOT in Presidential elections — a critical and frequently tested distinction.
• The practice of nominating members under Article 80(3) has included eminent personalities from fields like science (Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan) and public life.

solution.concept_anchor: Rajya Sabha — absolute veto, near-veto, and subordinate role across processes

statement_analysis.statement: Rajya Sabha has an absolute constitutional veto on Constitutional Amendment Bills under Article 368 — the bill cannot become law if Rajya Sabha refuses to pass it.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 368 requires each House to pass the amendment separately by special majority; no joint sitting is available for constitutional amendments. Rajya Sabha's refusal is final — it has an absolute veto.

statement_analysis.statement: Rajya Sabha has no role in the impeachment of a Supreme Court judge — only the Lok Sabha can initiate and adopt an address for removal.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 124(4) provides that an address for removal of a Supreme Court judge may be presented by either House of Parliament; Rajya Sabha has an equal initiating role, and the address must be adopted by both Houses.

statement_analysis.statement: On a Money Bill, Rajya Sabha is constitutionally reduced to a recommendatory role — it cannot amend or veto the bill, and its recommendations may be ignored by Lok Sabha.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 109 provides that Money Bills can only be introduced in Lok Sabha; Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations within 14 days; Lok Sabha may accept or reject any or all recommendations, and if Rajya Sabha does not return the bill in 14 days, it is deemed passed.

statement_analysis.statement: During a Financial Emergency under Article 360, Rajya Sabha alone can approve the proclamation if Lok Sabha stands dissolved — giving Rajya Sabha a solo approval role similar to its role under Article 356.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 360 (Financial Emergency) does not have the same Rajya Sabha-solo-approval provision as Article 356 (President's Rule). Financial Emergency requires both Houses' approval; if Lok Sabha is dissolved, the Financial Emergency proclamation's status is governed differently — Article 360 does not explicitly replicate Article 356's solo-Rajya Sabha provision.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who generalise 'Rajya Sabha permanence means it can approve all emergencies alone when Lok Sabha is dissolved' may mark both statements 3 and 4 as correct along with statements 1, reaching 'all four.'
elimination_logic: Statement 1 — Article 368's requirement for separate House passage with no joint sitting = absolute Rajya Sabha veto. Correct.
Statement 2 — Article 124(4) says 'either House' — Rajya Sabha has an equal initiating role in judge removal. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 3 — Article 109 reduces Rajya Sabha to a recommendatory role on Money Bills. Correct.
Statement 4 — Article 360 does not have the same Rajya Sabha-solo-approval provision as Article 356; Financial Emergency does not extend this solo power. Incorrect.
Two statements (1 and 3) are correct — select option (b): Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 is the entity-swap trap: swapping Article 356's unique provision (Rajya Sabha alone can approve President's Rule when Lok Sabha is dissolved) onto Article 360 (Financial Emergency), where no such equivalent provision exists. Students who learn the Article 356 rule may incorrectly apply it to all emergency types due to the generalised 'Rajya Sabha permanence' principle.
solution.final_explanation:
Rajya Sabha's legislative role ranges from absolute veto (constitutional amendments) to a mere recommendatory function (Money Bills) depending on the bill or process involved.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Rajya Sabha has an absolute veto on constitutional amendments — no joint sitting, no bypass mechanism.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 124(4) explicitly says either House can initiate a judge's removal address; Rajya Sabha has an equal role.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Money Bills reduce Rajya Sabha to advisory status — it can recommend within 14 days, but Lok Sabha controls the outcome entirely.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: The Rajya Sabha-alone approval provision is specific to Article 356 (President's Rule); Financial Emergency (Article 360) does not have an equivalent provision.

Value Addition:
• Rajya Sabha's power spectrum: Absolute veto (Article 368) > Equal power (ordinary bills, Financial Bills Category II) > Advisory role (Money Bills) > Exclusive triggering power (Articles 249, 312).
• Financial Emergency (Article 360) has never been proclaimed in India's constitutional history.
• Article 124(4) judge removal: the address must be presented in the same session and adopted by both Houses by a special majority (Judges (Inquiry) Act 1968 governs the procedure).
